faq1.a: MCP is an open protocol that standardizes how AI applications connect to external tools and data sources, letting models discover and call tools through a single consistent interface.

faq2.a: An MCP client inside an AI app connects to MCP servers over a transport such as stdio or streamable HTTP. Servers expose tools, resources, and prompts that the model can discover and invoke at runtime.

faq3.a: Servers expose capabilities like querying databases, calling APIs, reading files, browsing the web, or running domain-specific actions, turning external systems into tools an AI agent can use.

faq4.a: Developers building AI agents and assistants, plus clients like Claude, Cursor, and other MCP-compatible tools that let users plug in servers to extend what their AI can do.

faq5.q: How do I install an MCP server?
faq5.a: Add the server to your client's MCP configuration with its command or URL and any required credentials. The client then launches or connects to it and exposes its tools to the model.

faq6.a: Security depends on which servers you trust and the permissions you grant. Run only servers you trust, scope credentials narrowly, and review the tools a server exposes before connecting.

faq7.q: What's the difference between MCP and regular APIs?
faq7.a: A regular API is a bespoke integration per service. MCP is a standard layer on top, so any compliant client can discover and use any compliant server without custom glue code.

faq8.q: Can I build my own MCP server?
faq8.a: Yes. Using the official SDKs you can wrap any data source or tool as an MCP server, define its tools and resources, and connect it to any MCP-compatible client.

privacy.introduction: This policy describes the data handled by the ToolPlane web application. ToolPlane is self-hosted software, so the deployment you use—not the open-source project in general—determines where data is stored and which optional integrations are enabled.
privacy.operatorBody: The person or organization operating this ToolPlane instance is responsible for its accounts, infrastructure, backups, connected providers, and legal compliance. Ask that operator for deployment-specific details.
privacy.dataBody: The instance can store account details; workspace memberships and settings; encrypted deployment credentials and configuration; installed servers, skills, toolkits, sandboxes, and agents; conversation content and attachments; API-token hashes; and request, tool, error, and audit logs. Server logs and tool results may contain data you send to connected systems.
privacy.useBody: Data is used to authenticate users, operate workspaces and agent runtimes, route tool calls, provide observability, secure the service, troubleshoot failures, and maintain user preferences. ToolPlane does not include advertising trackers or sell personal data.
privacy.cookiesBody: ToolPlane uses essential cookies for signed-in sessions, language, and security, plus browser storage for interface preferences such as theme. Disabling these may prevent parts of the console from working.
privacy.sharingBody: When you configure model providers, MCP servers, connectors, email delivery, or other integrations, relevant prompts, tool inputs, outputs, identifiers, or files may be sent to those services under their own terms. An operator may also disclose data when required by law or necessary to protect users and the service.
privacy.retentionBody: Live data remains until a user or operator removes it, subject to workspace permissions and deployment settings. aboutMcp.anMcpModelContextProtocolServerIsASmallP:
An MCP (Model Context Protocol) server is a small program that exposes
        tools, data, and prompts to AI applications through a single standard
        interface. Instead of building a custom integration for every service,
        an AI app can connect to any MCP server and immediately use what it
        offers.
aboutMcp.aClientInsideTheAiAppConnectsToTheServer:
A client inside the AI app connects to the server over a transport such
        as stdio or streamable HTTP. The server advertises its capabilities —
        for example querying a database, calling an API, or reading files — and
        the model can discover and invoke them at runtime.
aboutMcp.becauseTheProtocolIsStandardizedTheSameS:
Because the protocol is standardized, the same server works across any
        MCP-compatible client, and developers can extend what their AI can do
        simply by adding more servers.
